title: the Gayatri in context
hook: earth, sky, heaven: an Upanishad counts the syllables and finds the Gayatri's first line

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: the frame said before the verse, Om, then bhur, bhuvah, svah, earth, the space between, the sky. Did you pause at a doorway before starting something? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

A teacher in an old Sanskrit text is playing a counting game. Bhumir, antariksham, dyauh. Earth, sky, heaven. Count the syllables, the text says: eight. And the first foot of the Gayatri, the first of its lines, also has eight. So, it says, whoever knows the Gayatri's first line wins whatever there is in the three worlds. It sounds like a riddle. It's the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, taking the verse apart line by line to see what each line holds. Today: the Gayatri in an Upanishad.
screen: `EARTH, SKY, HEAVEN.` → `COUNT THE SYLLABLES: EIGHT.` → `THE FIRST LINE HAS EIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad gives a whole section to the Gayatri. It goes line by line. The first line, it says, is matched by earth, sky and heaven: eight syllables, the three worlds. The second line is matched by the three kinds of Vedic verse, the rik, the yajus and the saman: eight syllables again, the whole of sacred speech. The third line is matched by the three breaths, prana, apana, vyana, the breath in, the breath out and the breath that moves through the body: eight syllables, the whole of life. Worlds, words, breath. Then the text does something surprising. It says the Gayatri has a fourth foot. It calls it the visible one, beyond all dust: the sun that blazes. Some readers put it this way: the three lines can be said, and the fourth can only be seen. And then the Upanishad explains the name. In paraphrase: the Gayatri protects the gayas, and the gayas are the breaths. Because it protects the breaths, it's called gayatri. That's the Upanishad's own reading of the word, offered as a meditation more than a dictionary entry. Put together, it's a big claim made very plainly. This one short verse, in the Upanishad's eyes, holds the worlds, the scriptures and the breath of life, and points past itself to a light beyond the dust. It takes the verse we've been placing in its hymn and its practice, and places it inside the whole of things.
screen: `EARTH, SKY, HEAVEN: EIGHT SYLLABLES.` · `WORLDS, WORDS, BREATH.` · `A FOURTH FOOT: THE SUN THAT BLAZES.` · `IT GUARDS THE BREATHS, SAYS THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three breaths, and a fourth thing. Sit, and follow one in-breath all the way in. Then one out-breath all the way out. Then notice the breath that moves through the body: the small motion in the chest, the belly, the shoulders. In, out, through. Keep cycling through those three, slowly. Every so often, between breaths, leave a gap and notice whatever light there is: on your eyelids, in the room, at the window. Don't name it. Just notice it, and return to the breath. If you pray, you can hold the Gayatri's meaning as you go. The bell holds the time.

The Gayatri in context. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, its three lines hold the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths, and a fourth foot is the blazing sun. It protects the breaths, the text says. Today's word.
Your line: the Gayatri in context. Today, three times, catch your breath going in, going out, and moving through, and let it count as a line of the verse. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the Upanishads' readings of the Gayatri as a guide for meditation, contemplating the worlds, the Vedas and the breath while reciting or holding the verse.

fork.setup: you've matched three lines to the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths. the Upanishad keeps going. what does it add?
options: a fourth foot, the blazing sun
a warning never to recite it
fork.reveal: a fourth foot, the visible one, beyond all dust: the sun that blazes.

original.note: Sanskrit: breath, life-breath; in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad the Gayatri is said to protect the breaths.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gayatri is three lines and that's all.
what it means: the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad reads each line as holding a whole world, and names a fourth foot beyond them.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 5.14 calls the fourth foot darshatam padam paro-rajas, the visible foot beyond the dust, and explains gayatri as the one that protects the gayas, the breaths.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.14.1–3 (the three feet of the Gayatri: earth, sky, heaven; rik, yajus, saman; prana, apana, vyana; a fourth foot, the blazing sun)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.14.4 (it protects the gayas, the breaths; therefore it is called gayatri)

notes: Brihadaranyaka 5.14 (Madhyandina numbering may differ) paraphrased from memory: eight-syllable correspondences for each foot, the fourth foot 'darshatam padam paro-rajah', and the name explained as protecting the gayas (pranas). The glosses of prana, apana, vyana as in-breath, out-breath and the breath moving through the body follow common usage; schools differ on prana/apana direction. Confirm wording.
